conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you've been having some nausea and pain in your right side?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it started a few days ago. I’ve had low-grade fevers and night sweats. The pain is constant in my upper right abdomen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That sounds similar to your past cholangitis episodes. Any vomiting or changes in bowel movements?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting. No diarrhea or constipation. I just haven’t been eating much because I feel nauseous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We checked your labs and your alkaline phosphatase is elevated, which supports cholangitis. We’re starting you on meropenem to treat the infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember that antibiotic from last time. Is this another flare-up like before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it looks like recurrent cholangitis, likely due to your PSC. We’ll monitor your response and do some imaging tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your ultrasound showed a cirrhotic liver with splenomegaly and a small amount of ascites. No bile duct dilation, which is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is the ascites new? I didn’t feel more bloated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s small and likely chronic. We’re not doing a paracentesis now since your fever points to cholangitis, not a peritoneal infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. Should I be worried about infection in the fluid later?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you get fever again with ascites, we’d need to check it. For now, we’re focused on treating the bile duct infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We got your MRCP results. It shows the same beaded bile ducts from your PSC, no new stones. The portal vein is open, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So nothing changed since last time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No concerning changes. The stone we saw before isn’t visible now—might have passed. We’ll keep you on antibiotics for two weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need IV antibiotics the whole time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll switch you to ertapenem, which you can get through a PICC line at home. A procedure team will place it tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve never had a PICC before. Is it safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s very common. It’s a small tube in your arm vein that goes to a large vein near your heart. We’ll make sure it’s placed safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, the PICC was placed successfully in your left arm. You’ll get ertapenem through it once daily for nine more doses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Does it hurt? I feel some pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Some soreness is normal. We’ll keep the site clean and check it daily. You’ll get home health nursing to help with the infusions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my diuretics? I was on spironolactone and furosemide.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We increased both—spironolactone to 50 mg twice daily and furosemide to 40 mg twice daily—to help with fluid buildup.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I watch for swelling or weight gain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and check your potassium. We’ll do a basic metabolic panel at your follow-up to monitor electrolytes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your fever is gone, and you’re eating better. That’s a good sign the antibiotics are working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel much better. Do I still need the endoscopy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we scheduled it for today. You had a variceal bleed recently, so we need to check your esophagus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The EGD is done. You have grade II varices, but they’re not bleeding. No new bands were needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Grade II? Is that worse than before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s stable. You had grade III with bleeding last time. These are smaller and not actively bleeding, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I restart the rifaximin I was on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We held it during IV antibiotics. You can restart it after finishing ertapenem to prevent bacterial overgrowth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And nadolol? My last doctor wanted me on it for varices.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given your history of breathing trouble on it and bronchitis, we’re not restarting it. We’ll discuss risks at your liver clinic visit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re planning to discharge you this morning. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. No pain, no fever. Just ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll finish the ertapenem at home through the PICC. A nurse will come daily. When it’s done, the line will be removed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How long will that take?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nine more doses—about nine days. Then the home team removes the line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll see your liver doctor in two weeks. They’ll decide if you need long-term antibiotic prophylaxis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the endoscopy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Repeat EGD in three months to monitor the varices. Call if you have black stools or vomiting blood.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Any restrictions with the PICC?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep the site dry. No swimming. Shower with a protective cover. Watch for redness, swelling, or fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue all your usual meds—ursodiol, cholestyramine, levothyroxine, and the diuretics as adjusted.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel confident going home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’re glad you’re feeling better. Call your doctor if anything changes before your follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. The discharge papers are ready, and your husband can bring the car around.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. I’m ready to go.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will review your meds and PICC care one more time before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll wait for her.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—keep taking the antibiotics as scheduled. Don’t skip doses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I won’t. I know how important they are.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’ll see you in follow-up. Feel better soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Just keep up the good work at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. Nurse is on her way.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll wait right here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re all set.
